"I don't think the authors of the tweets I'm responding to would disagree with any of this, but saying "QA is valid" and "QA is not a stepping stone" isn't enough. We first need to ask "What does an industry where that is true look like?", then ask "What do we do to get there?"."

"So getting a QA department that solely wants to be QA and treating them like they're not disposable is removing a huge power imbalance that executives can leverage. To be blunt, they'd lose a huge union-busting tool, and they're not going to give it up easily."

"But, as stated, QA is the lowest-paid position. Any non-QA work studios can get out of QA while paying them at a QA rate is advantageous. And the dynamic from the reverse perspective is true: QA wanting to move up is often used against art/design/engineers to keep them in line."
"And hey, if they're thinking about hiring you they're likely going to need to vet your art/design/code chops too, so you might get some actual dev tasks to work on."

"As one of my current coworkers has phrased it, it's also a "trial period" for the studio. They get to see all the other soft skills that are needed to work as a dev without actually having you touch the game, like communication, organization, teamwork, and stress-management."

"Thing is, it's not an inaccurate statement; you get to be in close proximity with the devs (if they don't keep you in a separate building a la Epic), so you can talk with them, pick their brain, and maybe get mentorship on your work (which you're likely doing in your off-hours)."

"You can of course move directly into entry positions for design/art/code, but few design students I graduated with managed this, the ones that did were WAY better than me. Our professors reinforced this path as well, that starting in QA and moving up was also an option."

"You create this perception that QA is the most prominent path into being a dev. A LOT more people want to be designers, so just say becoming a designer is a lot easier if you pay your dues as a bug tester."

"The current way games are created and released, however, depends on this. A large number of QA is required for the final push, and it's not work that appeals to a terribly large number of people. So if you're a publisher, how do you encourage more people to fill positions needed?"
"Needless to say, it's WAY easier to get a design/art/programming position if you already have experience there. So if you're let go without having moved out of QA, you're pretty much back at zero."

"All with a clock ticking, and none of these outcomes are particularly likely. This dynamic, by the way, is still present with designers, artists, and engineers on contract who have full-time positions dangled in front of them as well."

"So, if you're trying to move into design, art, or programming (or don't want to go through the stress of finding another job), you have three options: try to move to the very small embedded QA, try to get promoted into art, design, etc., or try to do that while changing studios."

"There's a few positions at VV, "embedded QA", who are actually employed there and are persistent, as the name implies. But those positions are VERY scant; less than 10 while I was there. So if QA's your long-term path, then you're up against some pretty tough odds."

"And at the end of the project, they're just... all let go. Activision also won't hire you for 3 months at any of their studios if you have a contract that expires with them, so you'll need to try and find work at some other studio in the area, or work outside the industry again."

"Which is to say, yes, most people in QA viewed it as a stepping stone. Others were dispassionate about the work, and the rest were already in embedded QA. I think I heard about a grand total of one person being promoted to embedded while there."

"But actually talking with my coworkers, I don't know anybody that did; everyone was trying to move to art, engineering, or design, while a smaller subset of others just fell into it because they needed work. My lead there was an English major, for instance."

"I'm not sure if there's a technical definition for "layoff" but functionally that's what it is; the vast majority of a department just wiped out. Thing is, that's just how large studios operate; bulk up on temp QA workers as you approach release candidate, then let them go."

"Activision hired most of these people in several waves, with more getting added as the release date approached. The game was set to go gold in July for a September ship date. Some had contracts that expired at the end of August (like myself), others in October."

"I speak mostly from my experience at Vicarious Visions, as it's the only studio I've been at that's had a sizeable QA force (80 before release candidate, I think). I was only there for 3 months during a summer, so I would've been excluded from that survey for making only $5k."
